artboards.title: New thread — born into a route

annotations.text:
Setup is a trust ladder, not a wizard to rush.
Each rung adds exactly one power, and the app refuses to claim a capability it cannot actually serve. Nothing streams off this phone until rung 5 grants something to a named profile.

Every screen carries (gateway, profile, session).
The capsule at the top is never hidden, because the same profile name can exist on two gateways — @ash on Home and @ash-cloud on Cloud are different agents with different grants. Switching gateways restores that gateway's own last profile and session.

Activity is the lane that does not exist in the code yet, and it is the one that makes the rest debuggable.

Every phone event walks captured → uploaded → acked → judged → notified | suppressed | failed. Suppressed is a decision on the record, openable to see why. Failed stays pending and retries; it is never quietly marked handled.

A gateway outage never merges routes: each keeps its own queue depth, its own stale clock, its own ack watermark.

The rail and two panes are what Shell.kt already switches to above the compact width. The third column — run, node, queue — is a proposal, not something the code implies: at this width a control room can show what it is doing without you leaving the conversation.

A thread is not a chat window — it is a route with a transcript.
It is created into an exact (gateway, profile, session) and can never drift out of it, which is why the new-thread sheet makes you pick the gateway before you can name the thread. Model lock is per thread: a long-running thread keeps its model even when the profile default moves under it.

The switcher is the fast path between agents. Each gateway remembers its own last profile and thread, so coming back to Cloud does not drop you wherever you were on Home.

These two screens are the halves of one question: what does this phone tell Hermes, and what is Hermes allowed to do about it.

Every source has four settings, not a checkbox — stream full, summarise, count only, ignore — because "the agent should know something happened" and "the agent should read my messages" are different consents. Redaction runs on-device before upload, so the level you pick changes the payload the gateway ever sees; the sample updates as you cycle it.

Ignore means the event never leaves, not even as a count. Pause means it queues locally and goes in order later — nothing is dropped to make a graph look calm.

Three surfaces OpenClaw's shipped node app has and this concept did not.

The composer has four mutually exclusive paths, not one: typing, on-device dictation, a voice note that travels as audio, and realtime Talk that holds the microphone through the foreground service. Tap the mic to cycle the first three; the waveform enters Talk. Listen (TTS) sits on the assistant message, not in the composer.

The workspace is read-only on purpose: the agent writes there, the phone looks.

And a question is not an approval. An approval grants a capability; a question picks a branch. First answer wins and locks it for every other device; an expired question lets the run take its stated default.

The outbox already existed for events coming off the phone. This is the other direction — what you send.

The state worth designing is not queued or sent, it is "no answer": written, transmitted, never acknowledged. It may have landed. Retrying replays the same idempotency key so a duplicate cannot be created, and dropping it is an explicit choice with a stated consequence. Silent auto-retry would be the wrong answer here.

Settings is where the per-capability lease decision surfaces: gateways stay connected simultaneously and keep their own grants, but exclusive hardware is held by one of them at a time, with the holder named. Older gateways hide the features they cannot serve instead of failing when tapped.
